title: Phonon-Mediated Thermal Transport in Nanocrystalline Silicon Using Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
authors: Houssem Rezgui, Catalina Coll Benejam, Miguel Pruneda, Clivia M. Sotomayor Torres
abstract: Understanding phonon-mediated heat transport in structurally complex materials remains a central challenge for next-generation electronic and nanomechanical devices, where grain boundaries and interfacial disorder strongly limit thermal dissipation. Although classical interatomic potentials enable large-scale simulations, their limited transferability can lead to inaccuracies in vibrational properties and interfacial phonon scattering. In this work, we develop a machine-learning based framework for modeling thermal transport in bulk and nanocrystalline silicon by combining Gaussian approximation potential (GAP) and multi-atomic cluster expansion (MACE) models with lattice-dynamical calculations and non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD). Harmonic and anharmonic force constants derived from machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are used within a unified Phonopy/Phono3py workflow to compute phonon dispersions, lifetimes, and lattice thermal conductivity, providing an internally consistent description of vibrational properties. In nanocrystalline silicon, NEMD simulations directly quantify the thermal boundary resistance associated with grain boundaries and reveal its sensitivity to interfacial roughness and the underlying interatomic description. Compared with the Stillinger-Weber and Tersoff potentials, the MLIPs provide a more accurate and internally consistent description of bulk and interfacial phonon transport, enabling more predictive modeling of nanoscale thermal transport in low-dimensional materials.
summary: This work establishes a robust machine-learning framework using potentials like GAP and MACE to simulate phonon-mediated heat transport in silicon. By applying this to nanocrystalline structures, the authors demonstrate that MLIPs accurately capture bulk vibrational properties while quantifying how grain boundary disorder limits thermal conductivity via NEMD simulations.
main_problem: Understanding phonon-mediated heat transport in complex materials, particularly where grain boundaries limit thermal dissipation for nanoscale devices.
main_result: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) provide a more accurate and internally consistent description of bulk and interfacial phonon transport compared to classical potentials. These MLIPs successfully model the temperature dependence of thermal conductivity across various structural defects.
method: The study develops and applies a comprehensive framework combining machine-learning potentials (GAP, MACE) with lattice dynamics calculations and Non-Equilibrium Molecular Dynamics (NEMD). This allows for the calculation of phonon properties and heat flow across interfaces.
model_or_system: The system studied is silicon (Si), examined in both bulk form and nanocrystalline/bicrystal structures featuring controlled grain boundaries. The methodology relies on training MLIPs using DFT data to accurately capture interatomic forces, enabling simulations of vibrational dynamics.
key_observables: Phonon dispersions, phonon lifetimes, lattice thermal conductivity ($\kappa$), thermal boundary resistance (TBR), and temperature profiles across interfaces.
important_parameters: Grain boundary misorientation angles ($10^\circ$ to $40^\circ$), interface roughness amplitudes ($A=1 	ext{ Å}, 2 	ext{ Å}, 3 	ext{ Å}$), and simulation temperatures (up to $350 	ext{ K}$).
main_assumptions: The accuracy of the thermal transport modeling hinges on the MLIPs providing an internally consistent description of vibrational properties derived from both bulk and interfacial regions.
figures_summary: Figures compare phonon DOS and dispersion relations between different potentials (MLIP vs. classical) against experiment, show $\kappa$ vs. T curves, and illustrate temperature profiles across interfaces with varying roughness amplitudes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from validating the MLIP framework in bulk silicon by comparing vibrational properties to established methods, then extends this validation to model structural disorder at grain boundaries using RDFs, culminating in NEMD simulations to quantify heat transfer limitations due to these interfaces.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter physics, the core methodology—developing and applying MLIPs for calculating complex many-body dynamics (phonons/heat flow)—is a prime example of advanced classical simulation techniques that bridge quantum mechanical accuracy with computational feasibility, relevant to numerical methods in AMO physics.
